title: Engineering Nonclassical States via the Dynamical Casimir Effect
authors: Maristella Crotti, Luca Razzoli, Giacomo Guarnieri, Luigi Giannelli, Giuseppe A. Falci, Giuliano Benenti
abstract: Nonadiabatic driving in ultrastrongly coupled light--matter systems is commonly regarded as a source of errors, as counter-rotating interactions convert vacuum fluctuations into real excitations through the dynamical Casimir effect (DCE). Here we show that, instead, the DCE can be harnessed as a resource for engineering nonclassical states of light. Considering a cavity mode ultrastrongly coupled to a frequency-tunable qubit, we employ optimal quantum control to design driving protocols that convert vacuum fluctuations into targeted states. Numerical optimization reveals a versatile and robust approach for the deterministic preparation of a broad class of nonclassical states, illustrated here through Fock states, squeezed states, and Schrödinger-cat-state superpositions.
summary: The paper shows how the Dynamical Casimir Effect, usually seen as an error mechanism in cavity-qubit systems, can be deliberately harnessed. By applying optimal quantum control techniques, the authors design precise driving pulses to deterministically generate high-fidelity nonclassical states like Fock and cat states. This demonstrates a powerful new paradigm for resource engineering in superconducting circuit QED.
main_problem: To utilize the Dynamical Casimir Effect (DCE) not as an error source, but actively as a resource to deterministically engineer nonclassical states of light.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated high-fidelity generation of various nonclassical states, including Fock and Schrödinger-cat states, by optimizing driving protocols in cavity-qubit systems.
method: Optimal quantum control techniques (CRAB and GRAPE) were employed to design time-dependent driving fields that steer the system evolution toward target quantum states.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a single-mode electromagnetic cavity ultrastrongly coupled to a frequency-tunable qubit. The dynamics are modeled using Hamiltonians incorporating counter-rotating terms, and open-system evolution is treated via the GKLS master equation.
key_observables: State fidelity (F), control cost, and Wigner functions plotted in phase space.
important_parameters: The system operates in the Ultrastrong Coupling (USC) regime; key parameters include coupling strengths ($g/\omega_c$) and environmental spectral densities ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on optimal control theory, assuming that the GKLS master equation accurately describes dissipation under weak system-bath coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the optimized driving protocols for generating specific states (e.g., $|n=6angle$), comparing Wigner functions across ideal, unitary, and open-system evolutions, and showing performance metrics versus noise levels or control parameters.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of harnessing DCE, details the Hamiltonian and system setup in the USC regime, applies optimal quantum control methods (CRAB/GRAPE) to design protocols, and finally presents results demonstrating high-fidelity state preparation while analyzing robustness against various noise sources.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges fundamental cavity QED physics with advanced quantum control theory. Showing that a process typically viewed as decoherence (DCE) can be controlled to create useful resources (nonclassical states) is a major advance for quantum optics and circuit QED platforms.

An external drive ΩD(t) modulates the qubit frequency, inducing dynam- ical Casimir photon generation in the USC regime. By opti- mally shaping the drive, target nonclassical cavity states can be generated deterministically from the quantum vacuum.

FIG. 3. Performance scaling of Fock-state generation with the target photon number n. Average (a) fidelity, and (b) control cost (4) as a function of n. Markers (mean value) and error bands (standard deviation) are obtained from 10 in- dependent unconstrained CRAB optimizations with different random seeds; the star markers indicate the performance of the optimal protocols obtained by refining the best CRAB so- lutions through a subsequent GRAPE optimization followed by a final pulse-smoothing interpolation step. The number of time intervals for the GRAPE refinement is Nt = 400, the other parameters are the same as those used in Fig. 2.

(b) Quantum noise: Fidelity as a function of the system–bath coupling strength η for Lindblad operators acting on the cavity (solid curve) and on the qubit (dashed curve).
